beats.headline: Why is your Stream pipeline doing nothing?
beats.subline: It isn't broken—it's lazy. Here is the anatomy of a Java stream.
beats.narration: If you think a Stream is just a fancy List, you are setting yourself up for bugs. Streams are lazy, single-use pipelines that hold zero data. Let's look at the anatomy.

beats.title: The Stream Lifecycle
beats.subtitle: Source -> Intermediate -> Terminal
beats.narration: Every pipeline needs a source, zero or more lazy intermediate operations, and exactly one terminal operation. The terminal operation is the only thing that actually triggers execution.

beats.title: Lazy Vertical Execution
beats.code:
list.stream()
    .filter(s -> { System.out.println("f: " + s); return true; })
    .map(s -> { System.out.println("m: " + s); return s; })
    .limit(1)
    .toList();

steps.explanation: Elements travel vertically through the entire chain. 'apple' hits filter, then map, before the next element is even touched.
limit(1) stops the pipeline immediately after the first element finishes, saving massive CPU cycles.

beats.narration: Streams execute vertically, not horizontally. Each element travels through the entire chain before the next one starts. This allows short-circuiting operations like limit to stop the entire process early.

beats.title: The Single-Use Trap
beats.caption: Streams close after the terminal op
beats.narration: Never reuse a stream variable. Once that terminal operation runs, the stream is closed. If you need multiple passes, create a new stream from the source or use a Supplier.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Stateful vs Stateless operations →
beats.narration: That is the foundation. In Part 2, we tackle the difference between stateless filters and stateful barriers like sorted.

beats.headline: Why does sorted() crash your app?
beats.subline: It is an unbounded stateful barrier. Here is why it eats your memory.
beats.narration: Why does sorted() sometimes crash your JVM with an OutOfMemoryError? Because it is a stateful barrier that must buffer every single element before it can emit the first one.

beats.title: Stateless vs Stateful

bottom.label: Stateful (sorted, distinct)
points: Can cause OOM on infinite streams

beats.narration: Stateless operations like filter process elements one by one. Stateful operations like sorted or distinct must remember everything they have seen, creating a memory barrier that can kill your performance.

beats.title: Optimize Your Pipeline Order

steps.explanation: Shrink the dataset before the expensive sort. Fewer items to sort means faster execution.
Sorting is O(n log n). Never sort the entire database if you only need the top 5.

beats.narration: Always filter before you sort. Shrinking the dataset first reduces the number of elements the sort operation has to buffer, keeping your memory footprint small and your performance high.

beats.title: The Infinite Stream Trap
beats.caption: Infinite streams + sorted = crash
beats.narration: Never call sorted on an infinite stream. Without a limit, it will buffer forever until the JVM runs out of heap space. Always constrain your data before applying stateful barriers.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.narration: You now know how to avoid memory traps. In Part 3, we master flatMap to flatten nested lists into single streams.

beats.headline: Stop nesting your streams.
beats.subline: flatMap is the secret to clean, readable data pipelines.
beats.narration: Stuck with a Stream of Lists? Don't use a double loop. Use flatMap to flatten nested structures into a single stream of elements.

beats.title: Map vs FlatMap
beats.subtitle: One-to-one vs One-to-many
beats.narration: Map is one-to-one. FlatMap is one-to-many. It takes a function that returns a stream for every element, then concatenates all those streams into one single flat result.

beats.title: Flattening Order Items

steps.explanation: Extracts the list of items from each order and turns them into a single continuous stream of items.
Avoids boxing overhead by using primitive streams for math operations.

beats.narration: Here, flatMap turns a stream of orders into a stream of items. Using mapToLong then lets us perform math without the performance penalty of boxing every number into a Long object.

beats.title: Empty Streams are Free
beats.caption: No null checks needed!

lines.text: // If items list is empty, flatMap does nothing

beats.narration: The best part? If an order has no items, flatMap just returns an empty stream. You avoid all those messy null checks and guard clauses in your business logic.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): When to avoid Streams →
beats.narration: You are a flatMap pro. In Part 4, we discuss the final rule: when a plain loop is actually better than a stream.

beats.headline: Stop using streams for everything.
beats.subline: Sometimes, a plain for-loop is just better engineering.
beats.narration: Streams are powerful, but they aren't a hammer for every nail. Sometimes, a plain for-loop is cleaner, faster, and much easier to debug.

beats.title: Stream vs Loop
beats.narration: Use a loop if you need to throw checked exceptions, track complex state, or return early from a method. Streams turn those simple tasks into a mess of try-catch blocks.

beats.title: The Debugging Nightmare

steps.explanation: Stepping through this in a debugger jumps through internal JDK classes, making it impossible to track local state.

beats.narration: Debugging a stream chain is a nightmare. You jump in and out of internal JDK frames. If you are debugging tricky logic, a loop lets you see your variables clearly at every step.

beats.title: The Golden Rule
beats.caption: Keep it simple

lines.text: If you have to re-read the stream twice...

beats.narration: The rule is simple: if you have to re-read your stream expression twice to understand it, refactor it into a loop or small helper methods. Your team will thank you.
